If the working theory that the rebel groups and the local authority have been collaborating is true, a massive breach like that would risk the exposure of the entire investigation and all of our assets.

We cannot discount the possibility that the rebels had advanced knowledge they would be spied upon. An investigation of our intelligence network for any possible leaks is underway. Meanwhile, Agent (CLASSIFIED) will be temporarily kept away from the public while they and their friends and relatives are investigated as well.
strings.GRO_INVESTIGATION.32.a: For the glory of the Vaterland. No matter how dark the night, the day always comes.
strings.GRO_INVESTIGATION.99.d:
Hans Hüttig had never pondered a Reich without Adolf Hitler. The thought seemed traitorous, apocalyptic. Hitler was ill, confined to a bed in Germania under the care of doctors more eager to entertain a spasmatic rotation of would-be-successors. Hüttig's stomach felt like a stone, and fat beads of sweat crawled over his sebum-slick brow. Hüttig felt cold - a cold so deep that the warmth of the African sun seemed somehow lesser and more bearable.

Hüttig strode to his desk through the ranks of droning fans and took out a form and a pen. Nothing would deter him. Hitler's vision for Ostafrika would be realized, but he just needed more proof - to drive his men harder and prise the sole, incontrovertible truth from Müller and Schenck's profligate fiefdoms.

In ordered lettering, Hüttig wrote to lagging investigators and idle officers. Each man would be replaced with a new, more competent official: one who would hurry the investigation and produce fast results in future endeavors, or suffer a similar fate to his predecessor. Simultaneously, the results of the investigation would be hurried to Reich immediately. The arms of a thin metal clock hammered at the hours, gliding from one o'clock to two, and welcoming a black cloud pregnant with rainwater.

Hüttig set his pen down and walked to his balcony. Even in a world without Hitler - without the man who led the Aryan race in war to become the masters of Europe - there would still be his rule. The indolent, the weak: all would be destroyed in the service of a great people and their magnificent German Reich.
strings.GRO_INVESTIGATION.100.d:
Reichskommissar Hüttig,

We have received your report and have studied it in full. As horrifying as such a conclusion is, we have no choice but to admit there is a strong likelihood that Reichskommissars Schenck and Müller have committed grave treason against the Reich.

The allegations that you made were unthinkable and shocking. As I'm sure you are aware, these allegations were ones that would require a great deal of proof. We admit there was widespread doubt initially as to the accuracy of your claims. However, the weight of your evidence is overwhelming. This office has concluded that your claims were made in good faith, and that it is not a misguided attempt to settle a personal grudge. The mountain of intelligence you have presented to us will go straight to the relevant authorities.

At the next possible opportunity, you will be summoned to Germania. There, we will discuss further investigations, and possible sanctions against the rogue Reichskommissariats. Unfortunately, the chaos of the attempt on our Füher's life prevents us from immediately having this meeting right now. You should, however, expect to leave for Germania at a moment's notice sometime in the next few months. Continue with all current investigations and evidence-gathering in the meantime. You and your agents have done the German Volk a great service.

Heil Hitler,

Philipp Bouhler

Chef der Kanzlei des Führers der NSDAP
strings.GRO_INVESTIGATION.101.d:
Reichskommissar Hüttig,

We have received your report and have studied it in full. Your conclusions are interesting, if a bit implausible, and warrant further research.

The allegations that you made were unthinkable and shocking. As I'm sure you are aware, these allegations were ones that would require a great deal of proof. Suffice to say, the evidence you put forward was enough to consider. The allegations are serious and further investigations do need to be conducted.

However, the Kanzlei has much more pressing concerns at the moment. Your case, though you do seem passionate about it, is extremely vague, and is not a high priority right now. We unfortunately have to put any further investigations off until a later date where we can fully commit ourselves to such an investigation. In the meantime, we order you to cease all further investigations until a full and proper one can be conducted. We will contact you if there is a change which causes us to reevaluate the importance of your investigation.

Heil Hitler,

Philipp Bouhler

Chef der Kanzlei des Führers der NSDAP
strings.GRO_INVESTIGATION.101.a: You don't know the true danger that we're in...
strings.GRO_INVESTIGATION.102.d:
Reichskommissar Hüttig,

We have received your report and have studied it in full. And we are appalled by the fact a Reichskommissar such as yourself would debase the office that you hold with such lies and allegations.

The two men you are accusing are honorable and exemplary members of the NSDAP, with spotless records. Reichskommissar Müller has defended the possessions of the Reich from the Cameroonian menace, and has provided a constant supply of income to the Reich even in our economic hardship. Reichskommissar Schenck is a heroic fighter ace with legendary exploits during the Second Weltkrieg and over Russia, and even now defends the Reich from its enemies in the Sahara. To attack them with such flimsy evidence is nothing short of disgraceful and unbecoming of a fellow Reichskommissar.

The Kanzlei will decide your fate in due time. A meeting to decide on sanctions for your action will be convened as soon as possible. Consider yourself to be in a precarious position. And prepare yourself for potential retirement or reassignment.

Heil Hitler,

Philipp Bouhler

Chef der Kanzlei des Führers der NSDAP
strings.GRO_INVESTIGATION.102.a: What sort of incompotent fools inhabit Germania?
strings.GRO_INVESTIGATION.103.d:
Being the middleman for Hüttig's correspondence with Germania was an unenviable task. Today, that task had fallen on the shoulders of Simon Wissmann, a once idealistic soldier in the Heimat whose transfer to Ostafrika has thoroughly obliterated his initial youthful enthusiasm. He had enlisted to fight the enemies of the Reich and claim more Lebensraum for it, yet here he was trembling with fear as he started to turn the doorknob to Hüttig's office, a fear greater than his father ever felt when fighting in Russia. After all, he knew that if the Reichskommissar was in a foul enough mood, Hüttig would cut him down faster than Yegorov's cannons ever could've. Deep breath, feign more bravery than you'd have to muster when running at a machine gun, and open the door.

“Heil Hitler!” The man shouted at the top of his lungs, saluting in the Reichskommissar's direction as he sat behind his desk. “Herr Reichskommissar, I came as fast as I could. What is the urgent matter you spoke of?” Please, please, please let it be a re-assignment from this hellhole.

In as foul a mood as ever, Hüttig gestured at a written letter on his table, and spoke in a tone that reeked with resentment. “I want this sent to Germania post-haste.” He declared, motioning for Simon to come closer as he continued to speak. “By the peerless eloquence of a true Aryan, I'll convince those stubborn imbeciles in Germania to finally rid me of Schenck and Müller.”

Picking up the note, the young soldier skimmed its contents. To his horror, he realized that there was nothing there - nothing of value at least. It was nothing but Hüttig insisting through a meandering word salad to replace his peers across the borders. No evidence, nothing. All his arguments could be summed in one word: “traitors”. Simon almost turned pale as he realized not only what the reaction would be in Germania, but also what Hüttig's reaction would be upon hearing the inevitable response. Taking his eyes off the accursed piece of paper, it took all the willpower in the world for Simon to maintain his posture.

“... Herr Reichskommissar, I shall have it sent to Germania immediately.”

Picking up the piece of paper, Simon turned around and briskly walked out of Hüttig's office. The sooner, the better, and he definitely did not want to be anywhere near this place when Germania's reply came - assuming they would even bother responding to this.
strings.GRO_INVESTIGATION.103.a: Few things are worse than believing one's own fairy tales.
strings.GRO_INVESTIGATION.104.d:
He was getting too old for this. Throughout his long and meritorious tenure as the head of the Führer's chancellery, Philipp Bouhler, few things had proven as frustrating as a certain Reichskommissar in Bouhlerstadt. If it wasn't direct correspondence, it'd been someone further down in the food chain having to deal with his requests and accusations.

As he got behind his desk that morning, few things could've made him long for retirement more than hearing that Hans Hüttig had sent him a personal message, supposed to be the smoking gun that would finally prove the validity of Hüttig's accusations against his opponents. Simply looking at the letter filled him with a tiredness that all the coffee in Kongo could remedy. Nonetheless, he reached for his letter opener and set about to read the letter.

For all the wrong reasons, Bouhler's sensation of tiredness was quickly removed from his body and replaced at first with bewilderment, then frustration, and then anger. This meandering tirade before his eyes was nothing short of deranged treason! Where there was supposed to be evidence proving guilt, he could find nothing but paragraph after paragraph of rambling nonsense and insistence that essentially based on Hüttig's feelings alone, Germania was to throw out two of the Fatherland's proudly serving Reichskommissars.

Finding restraint, he stopped himself from calling to Bouhlerstadt or even penning a response. Had he done so in the moment, he'd likely just have insisted on giving Hüttig the Sonderbehandlung treatment due to the obvious mental crippling that the sun in Africa had inflicted upon him. No, that'd merely fuel the fool's Jew-like victim complex. A far more fitting punishment would be to simply let his message fester in the rat wheel of the Chancellery's bureaucracy.

After collecting himself, he picked up his phone and rung up one of the lowly pencil-pushers at the bottom of the Chancellery's hierarchy. Hüttig was going to get nothing but silence from Germania, and that would drive him up the wall.

“Herr Erhard, I have a letter which I wish for one of your department's clerk's to attend to whenever time allows. Let the man know, this is certainly no urgent matter.”
strings.GRO_INVESTIGATION.104.a: And God willing, he'd get nothing but silence from Bouhlerstadt.
strings.GRO_INVESTIGATION.105.d:
Simon knew this day would come. When Hüttig realized why Germania had stonewalled him all this time, he'd been sent into a fury the likes of which had rarely been sent before. For what felt like an eternity, the staff in his compound had been treated to furious screams that could've overpowered an artillery bombardment in terms of decibel.

The other men in the SS quietly wondered what could've caused such fury, but none was stupid enough to enter Hüttig's office while he was in such a fit of rage. Wissman knew why, though, and knowing it certainly did not make him any more eager to deal with Hüttig, having by this point become something of an unofficial secretary to the monster of Africa. Then suddenly, silence. Blissful yet terrifying silence gripped the entire compound after God knows how long he'd been stuck in a fit of rage. Like so many times before, it once again fell upon the young SS man's shoulders to check up on his boss. Only this time, the journey towards Hüttig's office was accompanied with the faint hope that the bitter old bastard finally gave up the ghost.

As he opened the door, the sight that greeted him was enough to make the young man's eyes widen. Broken furniture, torn books and pieces of paper, and very visible marks on his desk from repeated strikes with some kind of object. Possibly the phone, given the sorry state of that thing. Behind the desk was the sorriest sod of them all. Red in the face, and sadly still breathing. Simon really wanted to leave, but before he could do so the Reichskommissar sprung back to life.

“The fucking treacherous swine in Germania betrayed me! They betrayed me!” Hüttig tried to shout, but at this point his voice was so hoarse that he sounded like he'd gone through all the cigarettes in Zentralafrika in the span of half an hour.

“Herr Reichskommissar, you look unwell. Can I get you some water?”, the involuntary intern asked almost out of human reflexiveness upon seeing the man in such a sorry state of affairs.

“Get out! Get out, get out, get out!”

Didn't need to tell him twice. Simon got out and shut the door behind him as fast as a heartbeat, half-worried that the loon would shoot him if he lingered a moment longer. As for Hüttig, he was a broken man. Betrayed by everyone, he had only one hope left. His Führer dead, he had only one choice left: take the matter in his own hands and purge the rot in Afrika.
strings.GRO_INVESTIGATION.105.a: Only the Führer himself could have saved me from these fools!
